seoTitle: How to Fix Outlook/Hotmail 'Too Many Requests' Error 429
metaDescription: Fix the Hotmail or Outlook 'Too Many Requests' error 429: what triggers the rate limit, the fixes that clear it fastest, and when it's actually an account block instead.
intro:
The Outlook or Hotmail "Too Many Requests" error 429 shows up when Microsoft's servers temporarily block your account activity because too many requests came in from your browser in a short window. Frequent refreshes, repeated login attempts, or a browser extension quietly hammering the login endpoint in the background are the usual triggers. It looks alarming, but it's a rate-limit protection, not an account lockout or a hack.

This guide works through the fixes in the order that clears it fastest: stale session data first, then whether a browser extension or a connected mail app is the real cause, before anything as drastic as switching networks.

steps.heading: Understand what's happening
steps.body:
Error 429 means too many requests were sent to the server in too short a time, and Microsoft's servers respond by temporarily blocking further requests to protect the service instead of letting it get overwhelmed. It's most often caused by cached login data, stale cookies, or a browser extension repeatedly triggering requests behind the scenes, not by anything unusual happening on your account.

That distinction matters for where you look first: your browser's stored data and connected apps, not your account security. If the block is a genuine security flag instead of a plain rate limit, it can take noticeably longer to clear, which the later steps cover.

steps.heading: Clear cache and cookies for Outlook or Hotmail specifically
steps.body: Open your browser's settings and go to Privacy and Security, then Third-party cookies, then See all site data. Search for Outlook or Hotmail in that list and delete the stored data tied to those sites instead of wiping your entire browser history. This clears the old session files that are the most common cause of a lingering 429, since a corrupted or outdated session token can keep triggering failed requests every time the page tries to refresh itself.

steps.heading: Check whether a connected app is polling your account
steps.body:
If another mail app or an IMAP/POP client is set up against the same Outlook or Hotmail account, it can quietly generate its own stream of sign-in and sync requests on top of what your browser sends, and stack toward the same rate limit. This is easy to miss because the browser looks like the only thing open.

Check your phone's mail app and any desktop client (Outlook desktop, Thunderbird, a POP-based backup tool) for accounts pointed at the same address. Pause or remove the connection temporarily and see if the browser error clears once that background traffic stops.

steps.heading: Disable browser extensions one at a time
steps.body: Go to your browser's Extensions section and disable extensions individually instead of all at once. Ad blockers, VPNs, and password managers are the most common culprits, since they can intercept or duplicate requests to Outlook's login endpoint without you noticing. Check Outlook again after disabling each one; this isolates exactly which extension is causing the conflict, rather than leaving you guessing after a blanket disable.

steps.heading: Test in Incognito mode, another browser, or another network
steps.body:
Open Outlook in an Incognito or Private window, which bypasses your regular cache and most extensions. If Outlook loads there, the cause was cached files or an extension, not your account or Microsoft's servers. A different browser (Firefox, Edge) narrows this further.

If it still fails everywhere, the block may be tied to your IP address rather than your browser. Switching networks, restarting your router, or trying mobile data assigns a new IP and can bypass a network-level block. Signing out of all active sessions from your Microsoft account's security settings clears any stale sessions still generating requests in the background.

steps.heading: Avoid the patterns that trigger it again
steps.body: Once you're back in, avoid rapid repeated refreshing or logging in and out in quick succession, since this is the most common way the rate limit gets triggered in the first place. If you use Outlook across several devices, stagger the logins instead of opening the same account everywhere at once. Simultaneous activity from multiple sessions and connected apps is exactly the pattern Microsoft's rate limiting is built to catch.

troubleshooting.problem: The 429 error keeps coming back even after clearing cache and cookies
troubleshooting.cause: A phone's mail app, a desktop client, or another tool still connected over IMAP or POP is generating its own sign-in and sync requests in the background.
troubleshooting.fix: Check every device and app signed into the account and temporarily remove or pause any IMAP/POP connection, then retest in the browser.

troubleshooting.problem: The error is still there after 24-48 hours
troubleshooting.cause: This is longer than a plain rate limit normally takes, which points to an account-level security block for unusual sign-in activity rather than a simple too-many-requests limit.
troubleshooting.fix: Use Microsoft's official Outlook.com account unblock flow, which asks for a verification code or a password change to lift a security block.

troubleshooting.problem: Multiple people or devices on the same account keep re-triggering the block
troubleshooting.cause: Simultaneous logins and refreshes from several devices, or a shared account used by more than one person, stack toward the same rate limit.
troubleshooting.fix: Stagger sign-ins, and sign out of sessions nobody is actively using from the account's security settings.

faq.question: How long does the 429 error usually last?
faq.answer: Often just minutes if it was triggered by rapid refreshing, since the rate limit resets on its own once requests stop. If it's tied to a flagged security event instead of ordinary rate limiting, it can take 24-48 hours, or require going through Microsoft's account unblock process.

faq.question: Does this error mean my account was hacked?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. It's more often tied to activity patterns like frequent refreshes, a misbehaving browser extension, or a connected app polling in the background, rather than a security breach.

faq.question: Can a connected app like a phone's mail client cause this?
faq.answer: Yes. Any app checking the account over IMAP or POP adds its own requests on top of whatever your browser sends, and can push the total over the limit without you noticing.

faq.question: Can using multiple devices at once cause this error?
faq.answer: Yes. Logging in and refreshing from several devices at the same time is one of the patterns the rate limit is designed to catch.

faq.question: Will clearing my cache delete my emails?
faq.answer: No. Clearing browser cache and cookies doesn't touch your emails, which stay stored on Microsoft's servers.

faq.question: How do I tell if a browser extension is causing the error?
faq.answer: Open Outlook in Incognito or Private mode, which disables most extensions by default. If the error disappears there, re-enable extensions one at a time in normal mode, checking Outlook after each one, until you find the culprit.

verifiedNote: Microsoft does not publish an official knowledge-base article specifically for the consumer-facing HTTP 429 'Too Many Requests' error. Checked in September 2026 against Microsoft's own Q&A forum threads on this exact error (answered by Microsoft-recognized advisors on a Microsoft-hosted property) and against Microsoft's official 'Unblock my Outlook.com account' support page, which covers the separate, longer-lasting security-block scenario. That check added the IMAP/POP connected-app cause, the 'sign out of everywhere' fix, and the 24-48 hour timeframe for a genuine security block, none of which were in the original draft, and corrected the claim that the error always clears within a few hours.
